The report also alleged that Super Micro Computer re-hired top executives who were directly involved in a previous accounting issue that led to a temporary Nasdaq delisting in 2018. By the time of the news report, the stock had fallen 55% from its March all-time high to $547.64.

In March 2026, the Department of Justice criminally indicted three individuals over export control failures. Those indicted included a Super Micro Computer board member named in the Hindenburg report and another company manager.

title: Rumble spent over $125 million on creators against $81 million in revenue
points: The report said Rumble spent over $125 million on programming and content in 2023, against $81 million in revenue.
Pelican Way argued Rumble was worth less than $5 per share, about half its then-current price.
It cited a $3.0 billion market cap as of February 28, 2025, versus a $1.47 billion streaming valuation.
body: Rumble Inc. is a US video-sharing platform founded by Chris Pavlovski as an alternative to YouTube. It promoted user growth and new monetization products, and in December 2024 Tether made a $775 million strategic investment in the company.

In March 2025, Pelican Way Research published a short report questioning Rumble's valuation and operations. Pelican Way held a short position, so it earned if the shares fell. It reviewed SEC filings, earnings calls and creator spending.

The report said Rumble spent over $125 million on programming and content in 2023, against $81 million in revenue. It alleged that monthly active users had declined despite management claims, and questioned Rumble's new monetization products.

Pelican Way argued Rumble was worth less than $5 per share, about half its then-current price. It cited a $3.0 billion market cap as of February 28, 2025, versus a $1.47 billion streaming valuation. These were valuation estimates, not cash losses.
Rumble's net loss had widened to $80.3 million from $30.2 million the prior year.

title: Rocket Lab targeted a mid-2025 launch. Its shares fell over 10% after a warning.
points: The firm reviewed documents and conducted 23 interviews with industry experts, including former Rocket Lab engineers and executives.
Rocket Lab had $504 million in cash as of September, according to the report.
Rocket Lab shares fell over 10% during trading on February 25.
body: Rocket Lab is a US rocket developer that planned to launch Neutron, a medium-lift rocket designed to compete with SpaceX's Falcon 9. The company repeatedly told investors it expected Neutron to fly by mid-2025. Its shares had risen 485% over the previous year, giving it an $11.2 billion valuation.

On February 25, 2025, Bleecker Street Research alleged that Rocket Lab had misled investors about that schedule. The firm reviewed documents and conducted 23 interviews with industry experts, including former Rocket Lab engineers and executives. It said engine development, production, launch pad construction and rocket transport were behind schedule.

Bleecker Street argued that a launch in 2026 or 2027 could delay Rocket Lab's access to US national security launch contracts. Three aerospace executives estimated that completing Neutron and reaching profitability would cost $300-$600 million. Rocket Lab had $504 million in cash as of September, according to the report.

Bleecker Street disclosed that funds it managed held a short position, which would benefit from a falling share price. Rocket Lab shares fell over 10% during trading on February 25. The available reporting did not include a company response.

On February 25, 2025, law firm Block & Leviton announced an investigation into potential securities law violations at Rocket Lab. Its notice cited Bleecker Street's allegations about Neutron's launch schedule and the company's need for additional capital.

title: Cettire reported $12.5m Adj EBITDA with 30% from one-offs
points: The report alleged that 30% of the $12.5m figure came from one-offs: $1.2m in stock-based compensation, $1.6m in FX, and $0.8m in undisclosed other items.
Crash Capital also said Cettire held $23m in cash less working capital and would need a capital injection at its current run rate.
The shares fell 79.55% since the February 26, 2025 report.
body: Cettire Limited operates a digital marketplace specializing in high-end merchandise, distributing these products to customers across Australia and globally.

On February 26, 2025, short seller Crash Capital published a report stating that Cettire managed $12.5m Adj EBITDA, a 3.1% margin for the half. The report alleged that 30% of the $12.5m figure came from one-offs: $1.2m in stock-based compensation, $1.6m in FX, and $0.8m in undisclosed other items.
Crash Capital also said Cettire held $23m in cash less working capital and would need a capital injection at its current run rate. The shares fell 79.55% since the February 26, 2025 report.

On April 3, 2025, short seller Taxloss published a report stating that Cettire's market cap was $265m and that ending the US de minimis exemption would finish its US business. Taxloss wrote that Cettire's negative working capital of about $98m would consume its $101m cash balance if US sales scaled back.

title: Patients paid for licensed therapists. A short seller said they got AI.
points: The firm alleged that patients unknowingly received therapy from artificial intelligence.
Blue Orca wrote that BetterHelp warned on its website that AI therapy dehumanized patients and could harm their mental health.
News outlets reported the short position on February 19 and February 20, 2025.
body: Teladoc Health is listed on the New York Stock Exchange and runs the BetterHelp mental health platform. Patients on BetterHelp pay for therapy from licensed therapists.

On February 19, 2025, Blue Orca Capital published a report on its website and announced a short position in Teladoc, meaning it earns when the shares fall. The firm alleged that patients unknowingly received therapy from artificial intelligence.

Blue Orca wrote that BetterHelp warned on its website that AI therapy dehumanized patients and could harm their mental health. The report alleged that BetterHelp gave therapists perverse incentives to cut corners with AI, and that accounting maneuvers concealed that Teladoc was far less profitable and generated far less cash than investors were led to believe.
News outlets reported the short position on February 19 and February 20, 2025.

title: Corporate Travel forecast $220-$260m. Its auditor later flagged the accounts.
points: The report noted CTD historically issued next-year guidance at second-half results and had missed revised FY24 guidance, citing macro, politics and a UK contract.
Crash Capital also questioned CTD's statement that it made substantive supplier payments in December 2024.
The report also examined how CTD accounted for ~60% operating margins in FY25, and a tracker listed the shares down 78.62% since the initial report.
body: Corporate Travel Management is an Australian company that arranges travel for corporate clients. In February 2025, it issued early FY26 guidance of $220-$260m, above market expectations of $220m, and its shares rose 10% to 16.50 the day before February 19.

On February 19, 2025, Crash Capital published an analysis questioning the forecast, stating neither the author nor the firm held a long or short position. The report noted CTD historically issued next-year guidance at second-half results and had missed revised FY24 guidance, citing macro, politics and a UK contract.
Crash Capital also questioned CTD's statement that it made substantive supplier payments in December 2024. On May 4, 2025, the author wrote that CTD had never posted guidance 1.5 years early.

On September 29, 2025, Crash Capital reported that CTD had been in a trading halt since August after its newly appointed auditor flagged issues in its FY24 accounts requiring restatement. The report also examined how CTD accounted for ~60% operating margins in FY25, and a tracker listed the shares down 78.62% since the initial report.

title: Hims guided to $470 million in sales. Credit card data pointed to slowing core growth.
points: Hims shares jumped more than 10% intraday after an FDA committee vote on peptides, before closing around 3% higher at $32.74.
Cedar Grove closed its short position after first-quarter 2026 earnings and initiated a long position during the second quarter.
An October 7, 2026 article reported that Cedar Grove highlighted Hims in its third-quarter investor letter.
body: Hims & Hers Health is a US telehealth platform that sells curated prescription and non-prescription health products. It guided investors to fourth-quarter sales between $465 million and $470 million, alongside sell-side estimates of $469 million.

On February 18, 2025, Cedar Grove Capital Management published a report reiterating a short position, which profits when shares fall. Citing Bank of America commentary and Second Measure credit card data, it alleged that Hims' reliance on GLP-1 treatments exceeded the 26% net sales estimate and that core growth outside GLP-1s had decelerated.

On July 23, 2026, Hims shares jumped more than 10% intraday after an FDA committee vote on peptides, before closing around 3% higher at $32.74. Martin Shkreli publicly disclosed a short position against the move. Cedar Grove closed its short position after first-quarter 2026 earnings and initiated a long position during the second quarter.
On October 6, 2026, Hims closed at $29.47 with a $6.88 billion market capitalization. An October 7, 2026 article reported that Cedar Grove highlighted Hims in its third-quarter investor letter.

title: Pagaya sold loan risk to investors. Its own fund bought the riskiest part.
points: Iceberg also questioned Pagaya's claim that credit risk would improve in 2025.
Iceberg's February 18 report compared loan delinquency rates for 2024 and 2023 and said the newer loans performed no better.
A later Iceberg report stated that its short position had been covered on May 6, 2025.
body: Pagaya is a Nasdaq-listed fintech company that assesses consumer loans from banks and online lenders. It told investors that its AI could assess loans its partners had rejected and that it transferred most of the risk to investors through securities backed by those loans.

On February 11, 2025, short seller Iceberg Research alleged that Pagaya used a fund it managed to buy the riskiest portions of those securities. Iceberg examined 29 publicly rated transactions and found that many of the lowest-quality portions were unrated or had been downgraded as loan performance deteriorated.

Iceberg said some investors in the Opportunity Fund had struggled to withdraw their money. It cited a 2024 report by Israeli newspaper TheMarker that investors holding about $100 million of assets under management had questioned transactions that generated fees for Pagaya.

On February 18, Iceberg reported that Pagaya had recorded $229 million in credit-related impairments in the latest quarter, bringing the annual total to about $354 million. These were accounting charges, not investor withdrawals. Iceberg also questioned Pagaya's claim that credit risk would improve in 2025.

Iceberg's February 18 report compared loan delinquency rates for 2024 and 2023 and said the newer loans performed no better. A later Iceberg report stated that its short position had been covered on May 6, 2025.

title: GeneDx's revenue was allegedly inflated by 25% through insurance billing
points: It alleged that GeneDx used code stacking, a billing practice that combined codes to obtain higher insurance payments, and estimated that this inflated revenue by approximately 25%.
Grizzly also pointed to a 2022 dispute with UnitedHealthcare that resulted in a settlement to repay $42 million over four years.
Its reference to over $800 million in fines concerned other perpetrators, not a penalty imposed on GeneDx.
body: GeneDx is a US genetic testing company that specializes in tests for rare genetic disorders. Its shares had risen over 2,500% since the start of 2024, and its stock market value had reached $2 billion, compared with the approximately $330 million paid to acquire the business.

On February 5, 2025, short seller Grizzly Research published allegations based on former employee accounts, whistleblower testimony and litigation. It alleged that GeneDx used code stacking, a billing practice that combined codes to obtain higher insurance payments, and estimated that this inflated revenue by approximately 25%.

Grizzly also pointed to a 2022 dispute with UnitedHealthcare that resulted in a settlement to repay $42 million over four years. Former employees alleged that the billing practice continued, while whistleblowers described supposedly independent counseling entities that directed patients exclusively to GeneDx.

The report also described an undisclosed whistleblower action and warned that insurers might seek repayment. Its reference to over $800 million in fines concerned other perpetrators, not a penalty imposed on GeneDx. The supplied accounts gave neither the share price reaction on February 5 nor a company response.

On February 17, 2025, BMF Reports published another article about the alleged billing practices and potential overcharging of Medicare and Medicaid. It repeated the concerns about GeneDx's financial results but provided no subsequent regulatory finding or court decision.

title: Applied Optoelectronics projected $600 million in 800G sales. Short sellers found no samples.
points: Culper conducted more than 20 interviews with former employees, competitors, hyperscalers, and industry experts, and visited company facilities.
The report alleged that Applied Optoelectronics never shipped 800G samples in the third quarter of 2023 and had only planned a September 2024 release.
BMF Reports published a separate report alleging that a former Meta employee confirmed Applied Optoelectronics missed Meta's request window for 800G transceivers.
body: Applied Optoelectronics is a Nasdaq-listed manufacturer of optical transceivers and networking components for data centers and cable television equipment. The company told investors its 800G transceivers were undergoing customer qualifications worth $500 million to $600 million in expected sales, and said it had shipped samples to two customers in the third quarter of 2023.

On February 4, 2025, Culper Research published a report and said it held a short position, meaning it earns when the shares fall. Culper conducted more than 20 interviews with former employees, competitors, hyperscalers, and industry experts, and visited company facilities. The report alleged that Applied Optoelectronics never shipped 800G samples in the third quarter of 2023 and had only planned a September 2024 release.

Culper also alleged that the company had no disclosed 800G customers, lacked production capacity, and overstated a Microsoft agreement worth over $300 million that carried no minimum purchase obligations. On February 9, 2025, BMF Reports published a separate report alleging that a former Meta employee confirmed Applied Optoelectronics missed Meta's request window for 800G transceivers.
On April 10, 2026, Citron Research called the company's valuation delusional.

title: A 4,000-page rate filing pointed to $2 billion in wildfire claims for Mercury General
points: Wolfpack analyzed a June 2024 rate filing of about 4,000 pages and found Mercury General insured 929 homeowner policies in Altadena, where about 63% of single-family homes were destroyed.
The report alleged gross wildfire losses would exceed $2 billion, exhausting the $1.3 billion reinsurance tower.
Wolfpack published a second report calling Mercury General's earnings release misleading, noting the insurer had already paid out $800 million and excluded FAIR assessments from gross losses.
body: Mercury General is a US insurer. Following the Eaton and Palisades wildfires in Los Angeles, the company told investors it had $1.3 billion in reinsurance and could treat the fires as two separate events to gain an additional $1.2 billion in coverage.

On January 29, 2025, short seller Wolfpack Research published a report and disclosed it held a short position, which profits when shares fall. Wolfpack analyzed a June 2024 rate filing of about 4,000 pages and found Mercury General insured 929 homeowner policies in Altadena, where about 63% of single-family homes were destroyed.

The report alleged gross wildfire losses would exceed $2 billion, exhausting the $1.3 billion reinsurance tower. On February 12, 2025, Wolfpack published a second report calling Mercury General's earnings release misleading, noting the insurer had already paid out $800 million and excluded FAIR assessments from gross losses.

Wolfpack also stated Mercury General was the only carrier among four peers to include subrogation benefits in net loss figures and to estimate an average loss per homeowner policy at 57% of the peer average of $2.4 million.

title: AppLovin claimed nearly 100% incrementality. Short sellers estimated 25% to 35%.
points: On March 27 and March 28, 2025, Muddy Waters Research published reports and said it was short the stock.
Muddy Waters analyzed web traffic and code and alleged that about 52% of AppLovin's e-commerce conversions came from retargeting, with incrementality of only about 25% to 35%.
It also alleged that AppLovin extracted user IDs from Meta, Snap, TikTok, Reddit, and Google to build persistent user identifiers and observed e-commerce client churn of about 23% in Q1.
body: AppLovin is an advertising technology platform for mobile gaming apps and e-commerce. Its chief executive officer, Adam Foroughi, told investors on a Q3 2024 earnings call that clients were experiencing nearly 100% incrementality and claimed almost no client churn.

On February 26, 2025, Culper Research published a report after decompiling app code, interviewing former employees and customers, and sharing research with Fuzzy Panda Research. On March 27 and March 28, 2025, Muddy Waters Research published reports and said it was short the stock.

Muddy Waters analyzed web traffic and code and alleged that about 52% of AppLovin's e-commerce conversions came from retargeting, with incrementality of only about 25% to 35%. It also alleged that AppLovin extracted user IDs from Meta, Snap, TikTok, Reddit, and Google to build persistent user identifiers and observed e-commerce client churn of about 23% in Q1.

On March 31, 2025, Foroughi denied in a blog post that the company created or used persistent identifiers, referencing an analysis by chief technology officer Shikin. On May 7, 2025, Muddy Waters published a follow-up report alleging that those responses contained false statements and that AppLovin continued to use persistent identifiers.

title: Veritas said 40% of Brookfield's distributable earnings lacked cash flow backing
points: In 2025, Veritas Investment Research analysts Dimitry Khmelnitsky and Benjamin Butler examined Brookfield's own disclosures.
It also said Brookfield excluded cash costs and understated sustaining capital expenditures.
Veritas alleged that Brookfield used related-party insurance companies to offload assets at high valuations during challenging markets.
body: Brookfield Corporation is a conglomerate in Canada that pivoted into life insurance through Brookfield Wealth Solutions. Management told investors it aimed to grow its insurance assets from $110 billion to $300 billion by 2029, with the unit accounting for about 75% of expected Distributable Earnings growth through 2030.

In 2025, Veritas Investment Research analysts Dimitry Khmelnitsky and Benjamin Butler examined Brookfield's own disclosures. Veritas estimated that approximately 40% of Brookfield's Distributable Earnings lacked underlying cash flow backing, and were funded instead by return of capital, intercompany equity infusions, and subsidies. It also said Brookfield excluded cash costs and understated sustaining capital expenditures.

Veritas alleged that Brookfield used related-party insurance companies to offload assets at high valuations during challenging markets. On March 6, 2025, the Financial Times published an investigative feature on circular cash flows between Brookfield entities.

Nicholas Goodman, President and CFO of Brookfield Corporation, and Michael McRaith, Vice Chair of Brookfield Wealth Solutions, later presented the company's strategic response and business rationale during a webinar hosted by Veritas.

title: A $1.5 billion AI company relied on an undisclosed partner for revenue
points: According to a later shareholder derivative suit, the short-seller report about an undisclosed related party caused a record stock drop for the company.
A shareholder derivative suit had been filed against iLearningEngines executives, alleging they faked revenue through that undisclosed related party.
The suit also noted that the report had exposed the company to a proposed class action.
body: iLearningEngines Inc. is a Nasdaq-listed education software company that went public through a SPAC. It had reached a peak market valuation of about $1.5 billion.

In August 2024, short seller Hindenburg Research published a report titled "iLearningEngines: An Artificial Intelligence SPAC With Artificial Partners And Artificial Revenue." Hindenburg alleged that the company's partners and revenue were artificial.
According to a later shareholder derivative suit, the short-seller report about an undisclosed related party caused a record stock drop for the company.

By January 21, 2025, a shareholder derivative suit had been filed against iLearningEngines executives, alleging they faked revenue through that undisclosed related party. The suit also noted that the report had exposed the company to a proposed class action.

title: TransMedics shares fell 13% after allegations of organ trafficking and billing fraud
points: The report also alleged unreported device failures and widespread use of devices outside their approved purposes.
Scorpion Capital assigned the shares a target price of $0.
TransMedics shares fell 13% over two trading days following the report.
body: TransMedics is a medical device company that makes Organ Care System devices used in organ transplantation. Its business came under scrutiny after a short seller accused it of billing fraud, unsafe transplant practices and coercive dealings with customers.

On January 10, 2025, Scorpion Capital published a report alleging that TransMedics used kickbacks, fraudulent billing and pressure on customers. The report also alleged unreported device failures and widespread use of devices outside their approved purposes. Scorpion Capital assigned the shares a target price of $0.

TransMedics shares fell 13% over two trading days following the report. The company denied the allegations, called the report inaccurate and misleading, and accused Scorpion Capital of trying to manipulate the market for financial gain.

By January 16, 2025, shareholder rights firms Bragar Eagel & Squire and Hagens Berman Sobol Shapiro were investigating whether TransMedics had misled investors or withheld important information. A regulatory petition also requested that the FDA suspend approval of TransMedics Organ Care System devices, particularly the OCS Liver device.

title: Red Cat promised a $55 million Army contract. Officials put the deal at $12.9 million.
points: It reviewed US Army budget documents showing a 2025 program budget of just under $25 million, and Customs and Border Patrol procurement plans of $1 million.
Short seller Fuzzy Panda Research published its own report while holding a short position.

Citing former employees and defense officials, it alleged that 60% of Red Cat's drones initially failed to work and that competitor Skydio had already delivered hundreds of drones for the same Army program.
body: Red Cat Holdings is a US drone manufacturer that told investors it had won a sole-source US Army short-range reconnaissance contract. Management projected $80 million to $120 million in revenue for fiscal year 2025, claiming its initial production deal would exceed $55 million.

On January 16, 2025, short seller Kerrisdale Capital published a report questioning those projections, noting it held a short position and profited if the shares fell. It reviewed US Army budget documents showing a 2025 program budget of just under $25 million, and Customs and Border Patrol procurement plans of $1 million.

On August 15, 2025, short seller Fuzzy Panda Research published its own report while holding a short position. Citing former employees and defense officials, it alleged that 60% of Red Cat's drones initially failed to work and that competitor Skydio had already delivered hundreds of drones for the same Army program.

On October 10, 2025, Fuzzy Panda Research published follow-up findings after contacting Army officials. The report said Army officials confirmed the Low-Rate Initial Production contract was worth only $12.9 million, and that Red Cat drones had been in the NATO catalogue since November 2023 without significant sales.

title: SEALSQ raised $400 million at its spin-off, then lost 59% of its share price
points: BMF Reports published its own report examining SEALSQ's semiconductor business and crypto project.
BMF Reports noted that SEALSQ raised $400 million during its 2023 spin-off, but its shares fell from $14.73 in May 2023 to $5.99 on January 13, 2025, a 59% decline.
The $400 million was money raised at launch, while the 59% drop measured the fall in the share price.
body: SEALSQ Corp is a semiconductor company that spun off from WISeKey in 2023 and trades publicly under the ticker LAES. It told investors it had 1.6 billion semiconductors in the market, planned a global satellite network called WiseSAT, and launched a cryptocurrency called SEALCOIN.

On January 8, 2025, Martin Shkreli published a short report stating that SEALSQ had tried to ride the quantum computing wave. On January 13, 2025, BMF Reports published its own report examining SEALSQ's semiconductor business and crypto project.

BMF Reports alleged that the company rebranded off-the-shelf chips without manufacturing them and that SEALCOIN lacked technical details. It said the crypto project looked like a way to raise capital rather than a real technology breakthrough.

BMF Reports noted that SEALSQ raised $400 million during its 2023 spin-off, but its shares fell from $14.73 in May 2023 to $5.99 on January 13, 2025, a 59% decline. The $400 million was money raised at launch, while the 59% drop measured the fall in the share price.

title: Quantum Computing claimed a longstanding NASA tie. It held one $26,000 contract.
points: Short seller Martin Shkreli recommended shorting Quantum Computing Inc., listing its price at $17.49 and his fair value at $0.01.
Capybara alleged that NASA confirmed it had only a single $26,000 contract with the company for generic computer programming, where Quantum Computing Inc. was the sole bidder.
The report also alleged that employee separation agreements barred staff from speaking with the SEC.
body: Quantum Computing Inc. tells investors it has quantum capabilities, revenue deals, and a longstanding relationship with NASA. The company said it won two contracts directly with NASA and at least four subcontracts awarded by NASA.
On January 8, 2025, short seller Martin Shkreli recommended shorting Quantum Computing Inc., listing its price at $17.49 and his fair value at $0.01.

On January 16, 2025, Capybara Research published a report saying its affiliates take market positions in the companies it reports on. Capybara spoke with NASA personnel and prime contractors and checked government contract records.

Capybara alleged that NASA confirmed it had only a single $26,000 contract with the company for generic computer programming, where Quantum Computing Inc. was the sole bidder. The report also alleged that employee separation agreements barred staff from speaking with the SEC.

title: Short seller says Premier's Adjusted EBITDA is 40% lower than reported

body: IonQ is a US quantum computing company that told investors it had strong commercial demand and was delivering on technical milestones. In October 2020, executive Chapman claimed the company had a system with 32 perfect qubits.

On March 13, 2025, short seller Kerrisdale Capital published a report and said it held a short position, earning when the shares fall. Citing a former IonQ executive and academic lab data, the report alleged IonQ only had an 11-qubit machine in October 2020 and faced scaling delays.

On February 4, 2026, short seller Wolfpack Research published another report and said it was short the stock. Wolfpack alleged that Pentagon budget earmarks provided up to 86% of IonQ's revenue from 2022 to 2024 before being canceled in 2025, leaving a $54.6 million hole in anticipated quantum computing revenue.

Wolfpack also reported that eight IonQ insiders sold or authorized the sale of $396.6 million in stock under new trading plans after the Senate approved the fiscal 2025 budget. Those stock sales and the canceled $54.6 million in anticipated contract revenue are separate figures.

On February 4, 2026, IonQ denied Wolfpack's report as false, misleading, and unsubstantiated claims from a short seller trying to drive down its share price. The company said it was continuing to advance its position in quantum computing.

body: D-Wave Quantum Inc. is a Canadian quantum computing company that went public via a SPAC merger in 2022. It announced a quantum supremacy benchmark to investors.

title: Sezzle processed pharmacy payments. Eight sites later lost the option.
points: BMF Reports separately questioned Sezzle's lending to subprime borrowers and subscription enrollments, citing Sezzle Premium's $12.99 monthly fee.
Checkout screenshots from January 2 and January 20 showed the option disappearing, while a PharmStore representative said its Sezzle contract was canceled.
Two SEC information requests concerning Sezzle in late 2024 had received no B7A exemption, suggesting the company was likely not under SEC investigation.
body: Sezzle is a U.S. payment company that lets shoppers split purchases into four installments. It told customers it aimed to promote financial empowerment, while earning fees from merchants and consumers. BMF Reports said its revenue grew 71% year over year and that merchants paid 4% to 6% per transaction.

On January 2, 2025, The Bear Cave alleged that Sezzle helped unauthorized Canadian online pharmacies collect payments from U.S. customers. It checked checkout pages and found that PharmStore, CanPharm, Canada Drugs Direct and Planet Drugs Direct took credit card payments exclusively through Sezzle.

On January 21, 2025, BMF Reports separately questioned Sezzle's lending to subprime borrowers and subscription enrollments, citing Sezzle Premium's $12.99 monthly fee. Those claims were allegations, not regulatory findings.

That same day, The Bear Cave reported that Sezzle had stopped processing payments for eight identified pharmacy websites. Checkout screenshots from January 2 and January 20 showed the option disappearing, while a PharmStore representative said its Sezzle contract was canceled.
Two SEC information requests concerning Sezzle in late 2024 had received no B7A exemption, suggesting the company was likely not under SEC investigation.
